title: How to Convert Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay with Casual Loading and Salary Sacrifice Superannuation
description: Learn how to convert hourly pay to annual salary for a 38-hour week, including casual loading, super guarantee, and salary sacrifice superannuation. Estimate your take-home pay wit
salarySummary: For a 38-hour week, your annual gross pay is your hourly rate multiplied by 38 hours per week and 52 weeks, with super paid on top.

faqs.q: How does casual loading affect my annual pay?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra 25% paid on top of your base hourly rate to compensate for lack of paid leave. When you convert your hourly rate to annual pay, you must include this loading if you are a casual employee. For example, if your base rate is $26.44 per hour (the National Minimum Wage), casual loading brings it to $33.05 per hour. Multiply that by 38 hours and 52 weeks to get an annual gross of about $65,300 before super and tax. The Fair Work Ombudsman sets award rates that often include casual loading, so always check your award.

faqs.q: What is salary sacrifice superannuation and how does it work?
faqs.a: Salary sacrifice superannuation is an arrangement where you agree to forgo part of your before-tax salary in exchange for additional super contributions from your employer. This reduces your taxable income, so you pay less income tax, but the super contributions are still taxed at 15% within the fund (up to concessional caps). For example, if you earn $80,000 annually and salary sacrifice $10,000 into super, your taxable income drops to $70,000, saving you up to $3,000 in tax (depending on your marginal rate). The Australian Taxation Office caps these contributions at $30,000 per year (2026–27). Note that super guarantee contributions (the mandatory 12%) are paid on top of your ordinary earnings, and salary sacrifice superannuation is separate from that.

faqs.q: How is tax calculated on my annual salary?
faqs.a: Tax on your annual salary uses the 2026–27 resident tax rates: no tax on the first $18,200, then 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000, 30% on $45,001 to $135,000, 37% on $135,001 to $190,000, and 45% above $190,000. Plus a 2% Medicare levy (based on 2025–26 single reduction thresholds as 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed here). For example, a gross annual salary of $80,000 would have about $16,267 in tax and $1,600 in Medicare levy, leaving a take-home of about $62,133. This estimate assumes you claim the full tax-free threshold and have no other deductions or offsets. Salary sacrifice superannuation can lower your taxable income, reducing your tax bill.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Conversion

To convert your hourly rate to an annual figure, use the standard formula: **hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**. This gives your gross annual pay before tax, super, and other deductions. The calculation assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. For most full-time employees, a 38-hour week is the benchmark set by the Fair Work Act. If you work fewer or more hours, adjust the weekly figure accordingly.

For example, if your hourly rate is $30.00 and you work 38 hours per week, your annual gross pay is $30.00 × 38 × 52 = $59,280. This is the starting point for estimating your take-home pay and superannuation. Use [the timesheet](/) to quickly run this calculation with different rates and hours.

## The Role of Casual Loading

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of their base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave (annual leave, sick leave, etc.). The Fair Work Commission sets the National Minimum Wage, which from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour for permanent employees. For casuals, the minimum becomes $33.05 per hour including the 25% loading. When you use our timesheet, you enter your **base hourly rate** (the rate before casual loading). A checkbox then adds the 25% loading on top. Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading, as that would double-count it.

Award rates often specify a base rate and a separate casual loading. For example, if your award says your base rate is $28.00 and casual loading is $7.00, your total hourly pay is $35.00. Our calculator handles this automatically when you check the casual loading box. The annual conversion then uses the loaded rate. So if you are a casual earning $35.00 per hour for 38 hours, your annual gross is $35.00 × 38 × 52 = $69,160. This is higher than a permanent employee on the same base rate because of the loading. For more details on award rates, see our [pay guides](/blog).

## Super Guarantee and Salary Sacrifice Superannuation

Superannuation is paid **on top** of your ordinary earnings. The super guarantee rate is 12% of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 (2026–27). This means if your annual gross pay is $80,000, your employer must contribute an additional $9,600 into your super fund. The super is not deducted from your pay; it is an extra cost to the employer. However, if you earn above the maximum base, super only applies up to that limit.

**Salary sacrifice superannuation** is a separate arrangement where you agree to reduce your before-tax salary in exchange for extra employer super contributions. This lowers your taxable income, saving you income tax. For example, if you earn $80,000 and salary sacrifice $10,000 into super, your taxable income becomes $70,000. You still receive the mandatory 12% super on your ordinary earnings (which may be reduced if your salary sacrifice is structured as a reduction in ordinary earnings – check with your employer). The Australian Taxation Office caps concessional contributions at $30,000 per year (including the mandatory 12% and any salary sacrifice). Salary sacrifice superannuation can be a tax-effective way to boost your retirement savings, especially if you are in a higher tax bracket. Learn more about [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging).

## Tax and Take-Home Pay

Once you have your annual gross pay, you can estimate tax using the 2026–27 resident tax rates:
- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15% on the excess over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: $4,020 plus 30% on the excess over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: $31,020 plus 37% on the excess over $135,000
- $190,001+: $51,370 plus 45% on the excess over $190,000

Plus a Medicare levy of 2% (using 2025–26 single reduction thresholds as the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed here). For a single person earning $80,000, the tax is approximately $16,267 and the Medicare levy is $1,600, leaving $62,133 take-home. This does not include HELP repayments, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging. Salary sacrifice superannuation reduces your taxable income, so your take-home pay may be lower but your super balance grows. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) guide for more detailed estimates.

## Using the Timesheet

Our [the timesheet](/) is designed for quick conversions. Enter your base hourly rate (the rate before casual loading). If you are a casual employee, check the box to add 25% casual loading. The calculator then shows your annual gross, fortnightly pay, and estimated super and tax. Remember that the annual figure is an estimate based on a consistent 38-hour week. If your hours vary, use an average weekly figure. The calculator also shows your fortnightly pay (weekly × 2) to help with budgeting. For reference tables on minimum wage and award rates, see our [reference tables](/data).

### Important Notes
- The National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour for permanent employees, $33.05 for casuals including loading. These are minimums; your award or agreement may set higher rates.
- Super guarantee is 12% of ordinary earnings, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base.
- Tax estimates use the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed here.
- Salary sacrifice superannuation is not included in the calculator by default, but you can adjust your taxable income manually to see the effect.
- This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax. Always consult a qualified professional for your specific situation.
